newsitem.title: USA: Weather improves for Columbia landing in Florida.
newsitem.headline: Weather improves for Columbia landing in Florida.

text.p: Astronauts closed the payload bay doors on shuttle Columbia and finished stowing gear early on Thursday for their journey home as skies cleared over the orbiter's Florida landing strip.

Weather forecasts called for improving conditions in central Florida, which should allow the shuttle to land at 7:33 a.m. EST (1233 GMT), said a spokesman for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. If last-minute clouds developed, the astronauts had a second chance to land at Kennedy Space Centre at 9:10 a.m. EST (1410 GMT).

"If for some reason we don't land today, tomorrow the weather at Kennedy Space Centre looks much, much better than we thought in the past few days. The models are predicting good weather. But our plan is to get you down today," ground controller Curt Brown told the crew aboard Columbia.

NASA had earlier feared that a low-pressure system moving across Florida might force the shuttle to land at Edwards Air Force Base in California. NASA prefers to land the shuttles whenever possible at Kennedy Space Centre to avoid the additional $1 million cost of ferrying the shuttle from California to Florida.

Space agency officials ordered the orbiter's five-member crew to return to earth one day earlier than planned after a crucial navigation tool unexpectedly failed on Wednesday and weather conditions began to worsen at all of the shuttle's landing sites.
The decision to call Columbia home early also came after a stuck airlock hatch last weekend forced NASA to scrap a pair of planned spacewalks.

Ground controllers closely watched as shuttle astronaut Tammy Jernigan and the rest of the crew closed Columbia's cargo bay doors shortly before 4 a.m. EST (0900 GMT). The doors have always operated smoothly on NASA's previous 79 shuttle flights, but had there been a problem the astronauts would have had to pry open the stuck hatch and make a spacewalk to manually crank the doors closed.
During the night, shuttle commander Ken Cockrell tested all 38 steering jets on the orbiter to make sure they were working for Columbia's high-speed landing.
The latest technical problem knocked out one of the shuttle's three crucial navigation units, known as inertial measurement units.

Although NASA flight director Wayne Hale said the "primary factor" for the crew's early return was the weather, he acknowledged the two equipment problems also played a role. "They certainly indicate that you ought to button things up and be prepared to come down at the earliest opportunity," he said, referring to the stuck hatch and the broken navigation unit.
